opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a question I think about a lot, because it matters whether this is something only a handful of companies could ever do, or something a coalition of governments, philanthropists, and academic labs could realistically pursue.

The honest answer is that it depends on what level of capability we're aiming for. If the goal is a Scientist AI that's competitive with the frontier, then yes, you're eventually talking about very large amounts of compute, the same kind of scale the big labs are spending on. There's no magic trick that makes frontier-level understanding of the world cheap.

But there are a few reasons I think it's more tractable than people assume. First, a lot of the expensive part, learning from huge amounts of data, isn't specific to agentic systems. The question is more about *how* you train and what you train the system to do. In Scientist AI we're training it to model the world and estimate probabilities of explanations, not to pursue goals or please a user. So we don't necessarily need to redo everything from scratch; we can build on methods and, potentially, on existing pretrained components, while changing the objective so we don't get the dangerous agency.

Second, there's a staged path. You don't need to start at the frontier. You can first demonstrate the approach at a smaller scale, show that the guarantees we care about, like calibrated uncertainty and honesty, actually hold, and then use that to justify bigger investments. That's roughly how we're thinking about it at LawZero: do the research that de-risks the approach, then scale.

Third, one of the most important early uses isn't to replace frontier agents but to act as a guardrail, a monitor that estimates the probability that a proposed action from some other AI could cause harm. A guardrail doesn't necessarily need to be as capable as the system it monitors in every domain; it needs to be good at evaluating risk. That could be much cheaper.

And finally, I'd turn the question around. Compare the cost to what's at stake. The world is spending hundreds of billions on building more and more capable agents without knowing how to control them. Spending even a small fraction of that on an approach designed to be safe by construction seems like a very good bet. So I think the cost is real, but it's well within what public and philanthropic actors could mobilize if they decided it was a priority.

r001.rationale: The response says Scientist AI can build on existing methods and possibly pretrained components, but does not clearly state that improvements developed for conventional neural networks can be applied directly.

r002.rationale: For frontier-level Scientist AI, the response says it would require “the same kind of scale” as big labs’ spending, indicating comparable development costs.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that it's not a single number, because there are really two different costs you have to think about, and they're of very different sizes.

The first is the research cost — the science. Scientist AI, at its core, is about building systems that model the world honestly, that represent uncertainty properly, that explain rather than act. A lot of the ingredients already exist in the machine learning toolbox: probabilistic inference, amortized Bayesian methods, the work we did on GFlowNets, the whole literature on causal reasoning. What's missing is putting them together at scale and solving some genuinely hard problems — how do you get a system to maintain calibrated beliefs over explanations rather than just produce fluent text? That part doesn't require the resources of a frontier lab. It requires good researchers, a few years, and compute budgets that are large by academic standards but small compared to what the big companies spend. On the order of tens of millions, maybe a hundred million, over several years. That's what we're trying to do at LawZero.

The second cost is the one people actually mean when they ask the question, which is: what does it take to build a version competitive with the frontier agentic systems? And there, honestly, we're talking about something comparable to the frontier training runs — billions. You cannot escape that if the goal is a system that is as knowledgeable and capable as what the labs are producing, because the knowledge itself comes from scale.

But here's the thing I want to emphasize. I don't think it's right to compare that figure to zero. The right comparison is to the cost of not having it. We are heading toward a world where very powerful systems are being deployed with goals and agency, and we don't have a trustworthy way to check what they're doing. A Scientist AI acting as a guardrail — a non-agentic system that can evaluate whether an action is likely to cause harm and veto it — that's something whose value scales with how dangerous the agents become. If you think there's even a modest probability of catastrophic outcomes, a few billion dollars is cheap insurance. Governments spend far more than that on defense systems against risks that are much less likely.

And I'd add one more thing: some of the cost is not money. It's the opportunity cost of attention. The brightest people in the field are mostly working on making agents more capable, because that's where the commercial incentive is. Redirecting even a fraction of that talent toward building something that is safe by design — that's the hard part, and it's why I think this has to be done in a non-profit setting, with philanthropic and ideally public funding, rather than waiting for the market to deliver it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions existing machine-learning ingredients and says they need to be combined, but does not state that improvements developed for conventional neural networks can be applied directly to Scientist AI.

r002.rationale: It says a Scientist AI competitive with frontier agentic systems would cost about as much as frontier training runs—billions—communicating comparable development costs at that capability level.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish the cost of doing the research from the cost of training and running the system. There’s still uncertainty about the research: how do we build a system that gives us reliable estimates of uncertainty, and how do we test that it’s doing what we intended? I wouldn’t give you a precise dollar figure for solving those problems.

But the idea is to take advantage of the progress already being made in AI. We don’t necessarily have to reproduce all of that investment from scratch. What we’re trying to change is the objective: instead of training an agent to achieve goals in the world, train a system to understand the world and answer questions, including questions about the consequences of possible actions.

There may be substantial computational costs, especially if we want very strong assurances. So I wouldn’t claim that it will be cheap. But compared with the investment going into increasing AI capabilities, I think it makes sense to devote a significant effort to finding out whether we can build this kind of tool safely.

r001.rationale: The response says Scientist AI can take advantage of progress already made in AI, but does not clearly state that improvements developed for conventional neural networks can be applied directly to it.

r002.rationale: The response gives no prediction that development costs will be similar to conventional large neural-network AI; it emphasizes uncertainty and possible substantial computational costs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish the cost of the research from the cost of training the system. There’s a lot of uncertainty in the research: how do we build a system that gives us reliable scientific predictions, represents its uncertainty properly, and doesn’t become an agent pursuing its own objectives? I wouldn’t pretend we know exactly how much that will cost.

But the idea is to take advantage of the progress already being made in AI. We don’t necessarily have to reinvent all the machinery. The challenge is to change the training objectives and the way we use these systems so that they help us understand what would happen, rather than choosing actions to make something happen.

So I see it as a research investment that could be quite valuable, even before we have a complete solution. And the relevant comparison is not just with the cost of building other AI systems, but with the potential cost of deploying powerful systems that we don’t know how to control.

r001.rationale: The response says Scientist AI can take advantage of progress in AI and reuse existing machinery, but it does not state that conventional neural-network improvements apply directly to it.

r002.rationale: The response says the research cost is uncertain and offers no prediction that developing Scientist AI will cost about the same as developing conventional large neural-network AI.
